stages.title: What is a question?
stages.hook: Why is the sky blue? Why do cats purr? Who asks the best questions: you, or grown-ups?
explain: A question is a way of asking to find out. Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why or how.
Some questions have a quick answer. "What colour is the banana?" is one. Other questions are big and have many answers. "Why do people make friends?" is one.
Philosophy begins with big questions. A philosopher is a person who loves to ask them and think hard about the answers. You can be one too.

steps: Think: that is a big question, not a quick one.
Ask: why might sharing be good?
Listen to ideas from other people.

analogies.home: At home you ask, "Why is it dark at night?" Asking helps you learn.
analogies.nature: A child watches ants and asks, "Where are they going?" Looking and asking go together.
analogies.city: On a bus you may ask, "How does the bus know where to stop?" Questions are everywhere.

stages.mnemonic: Ask WHY, and give it a try!
terms: Words we use to ask and find out.
What we say to reply to a question.
A person who loves to ask big questions and think.
A small word that opens big thinking.

misc.wrong: Only grown-ups can ask good questions.
misc.right: Anyone can ask a good question, even a very young child.

stages.limits: Some big questions do not have one answer that everyone agrees on. That is fine.

stages.title: Thinking about right and wrong
stages.hook: You find a toy on the floor. It is not yours. What should you do?
explain: Right means good and kind. Wrong means hurtful or unkind. We think about right and wrong when we choose what to do.
Hitting is wrong because it hurts. Helping is right because it makes things better. Before we act, we can ask: "Will this hurt someone? Will this help someone?"
Sometimes it is hard to know. Then we can ask a grown-up we trust, or think about how others feel.

example.q: A girl sees a boy fall down. Should she help?
steps: Ask: will helping hurt anyone?
Ask: will it make him feel better?
Yes, helping is the kind choice.

analogies.home: At home, we put away toys so no one trips. That is a kind choice.
analogies.farm: On a farm, we feed the animals every day. They need us. That is a good choice.
analogies.sport: In a game, we play by the rules. That is fair and right.

terms: Not good because it hurts someone.
What we feel inside, like happy or sad.

misc.wrong: Right and wrong are only about getting in trouble.
misc.right: Right and wrong are about how our actions affect other people and ourselves, not only about getting caught.

stages.title: Honesty and truth
stages.hook: Can a story be fun and not be true? How can we tell what is true?
explain: Being honest means telling the truth. A true thing is what really happened or really is. A lie is when we say something we know is not true to trick someone.
Honesty matters because people trust us when we tell the truth. Trust is like a bridge between people. Lies can break the bridge.
Pretend stories are not lies. Stories, jokes and play are fine because everyone knows they are made up. A lie is when we want someone to believe something false.

example.q: You ate the last biscuit. Mum asks who did. What is the honest answer?
steps: Remember what really happened.
Say it: "I ate it."
Say sorry and maybe offer to help.

analogies.home: If you say "I did my homework" and you did, people can trust you.
analogies.city: A shopkeeper who gives the right change builds trust with customers.
analogies.nature: A trail sign that points the right way helps hikers. A wrong sign would mislead them.

stages.mnemonic: Truth is a bridge. Lies make it break.
terms: Saying something false to trick someone.
Believing someone will tell the truth and do what is right.
A made-up game or story that everyone knows is not real.

misc.wrong: A fairy tale is a lie.
misc.right: A fairy tale is a made-up story that everyone knows is pretend. A lie is meant to trick someone.

stages.limits: Sometimes people feel it is hard to tell the truth because they are afraid. Kind honesty is still possible.

trip.prompt: Look for what honesty means and why it matters.

stages.title: Fairness and sharing
stages.hook: There is one cake and four children. How could they share it so everyone is happy?
explain: Fair means treating people in a way that is right for everyone. Sharing means letting others have some or use something with us.
Sometimes fair means the same for everyone, like four equal pieces of cake. Sometimes fair means what each person needs. A child with a sore foot may need a seat.
Taking turns is fair. When we cannot agree, we can talk, ask what each one needs, and find a way that feels right to all.

example.q: Two children want one ball. How can they be fair?
steps: Say each wants a turn.
Take turns, or play together.
Check that both are happy.
example.a: They take turns or play together.

analogies.home: At dinner, everyone gets some of the fruit, not just one person.
analogies.sport: In a game, players take turns to bat.
analogies.farm: On a farm, all the animals get water, big or small.

terms: Treating people in a way that is right and just.
To let others have or use a part.
A chance to go, one after another.

misc.wrong: Fair always means everyone gets exactly the same.
misc.right: Often it does, but sometimes fair means giving each person what they need.

stages.limits: People sometimes disagree about what fair means. That is a real question that thinkers still discuss.

stages.title: Respect and kindness
stages.hook: How do you feel when someone says "please" or "thank you"? How do you feel when someone is rude?
explain: Respect means treating others as important. We listen, we do not shout or hurt, and we care for other people's things. Kindness means doing or saying things that help others feel good.
We can show respect and kindness in small ways: a smile, a hello, waiting our turn, saying thank you. We can also help someone who is sad.
Everyone deserves respect, even people who look, speak or live differently from us. We are all people with feelings.

example.q: A new child joins your class and is shy. What can you do?
steps: Notice they are alone.
Say hello and smile.
Invite them to play.

analogies.home: We knock before we enter a room.
analogies.city: We give a seat on the bus to someone who needs it.
analogies.nature: We are gentle with plants and animals.

stages.mnemonic: Kind words are like warm sun.
terms: Helping others feel good with what we do and say.
Using good manners like please and thank you.
To make someone part of the group.

misc.wrong: Respect means doing what everyone says.

stages.title: Friendship and responsibility
stages.hook: What makes a good friend? And what does it mean to be someone people can count on?
explain: A friend is someone we like, trust and have fun with. Good friends are kind, honest and help each other. Friends can be big or small, near or far.
Responsibility means doing what you should and what you said you would do. You feed your pet if you promised. You look after your own things. People can count on you.
When we make a mistake, being responsible also means saying sorry and trying to fix it. Friends forgive, too.

example.q: You promised to bring a ball to play. What should you do?
steps: Remember your promise.
Bring the ball.
If you cannot, tell your friend early.

analogies.home: A child waters the plant every day as a job.
analogies.farm: A child brings water to the animals each morning.
analogies.sport: A team member shows up for practice so others can count on them.

stages.mnemonic: A friend and a promise are for keeps.
terms: A person we like and trust.

stages.title: Understanding different opinions
stages.hook: Your friend says orange is the best fruit. You say mango. Who is right?
explain: An opinion is what a person thinks or feels. People can have different opinions. Some things are just tastes, like a favourite colour or fruit. Nobody is wrong about their own taste.
Other things are facts. A fact can be checked: a day has 24 hours. We can check facts by looking, measuring or asking a reliable source.
When we disagree, we listen first. We can say, "Tell me why you think so." We can change our mind if we learn something new, or keep our idea and still be kind.

example.q: Ayo says dogs are the best. Lina says cats. What is this?
steps: Is it a fact you can check?
No, it is about what they like.
So they have different opinions, and both can be fine.

analogies.home: At dinner, people like different foods.
analogies.music: Some people like drums best, others like flutes.
analogies.sport: Some like football and some like swimming.

stages.mnemonic: Listen, think, and be kind: that is how to open a mind.
terms: Something that can be checked and is true.
To hear and try to understand.

misc.wrong: If two people disagree, one must be bad.
misc.right: People can disagree and both be thoughtful and kind.

stages.limits: Some questions look like opinions but can be checked, and some look like facts but are about values. Thinkers discuss where the line is.

A fact: we can read it
questions.why: Facts can be checked, opinions are what people feel.

questions.q: Your friend says, "Everyone must like what I like." What is wrong with that?
o: People can like different things
Nothing, because most people agree
Because only older children can choose
Because liking things is a rule
questions.why: People have different tastes.

questions.q: How can we tell if something is a fact?
o: We can check it
We feel it strongly
Someone shouted it
It is old
questions.why: Checking is key.

panel.q: Is "Football is better than swimming" a fact?
o: No, it is an opinion about what people like
Yes, because more people play football
Yes, because it can be checked with a ruler
Yes, because teachers said so
panel.why: There is no check for "better" taste.

panel.q: Why do different people have different opinions?
o: They have different experiences and likes
Because some of them do not think
Because they do not like each other
Because only one of them is clever
panel.why: Different lives lead to different views.

panel.q: Someone gives an opinion you strongly disagree with. What can you do?
o: Listen, ask why, and answer calmly
Tell them they are wrong at once
Ignore them and change the subject
Wait until they stop and then argue loudly
panel.why: Calm talk respects them.

teach.model: An opinion is what someone thinks or likes. A fact can be checked. People can have different opinions and still be kind. For example, liking different fruits.

points.ask: What should we do when we disagree?

stages.title: Making thoughtful choices
stages.hook: You have a choice: finish your game or help a friend who is stuck. How do you decide?
explain: A choice is when we pick one way to act from more than one. Thoughtful choosing means stopping to think before we act.
We can ask three questions: What could happen? Who will be helped or hurt? Is it kind, fair and honest? Then we pick, and we are ready to say why.
After we choose, we can look back: Did it go well? What would I do next time? This is how we grow wise.

example.q: A child finds a lost mitten at school. What choices are there?
steps: Keep it, leave it, or help it find its owner.
Who will be happy? The owner.
Choose to ask the teacher where lost things go.

analogies.home: Before we cross a room full of toys, we look so we do not step on them.
analogies.city: Before crossing a road, we stop, look and listen.
analogies.nature: Before picking a flower, we ask: will we harm the plant?

stages.mnemonic: Stop. Think. Choose. Then see how it went!
terms: To use your mind to work something out.

misc.wrong: The first idea is always the best.
misc.right: It helps to stop and think of more than one choice.

trip.prompt: Find a simple idea about making a choice.

questions.q: What should we do before a big choice?
o: Stop and think
Run
Close our eyes
Shout
questions.why: Thinking first helps.

questions.q: Which question helps us choose well?
o: Who could be helped or hurt?
How fast can I do this?
Which choice will I get a prize for?
Who will see me do it?
questions.why: It looks at others.

questions.q: You find a wallet. What is a thoughtful choice?
o: Give it to an adult to return
Keep it, since you found it
Spend it on something nice
Leave it where it is and walk away
questions.why: Returning it is honest and kind.

questions.q: After we choose, what is good to do?
o: Look back and learn
Forget everything
Blame others
Hide
questions.why: Looking back helps us grow.

questions.q: Why is it good to think of more than one choice?
o: One may be better than the first idea
Because the first idea is always wrong
Because choices must be many to count
Because it makes the choice take longer
questions.why: More choices may include a better one.

questions.q: A friend says "just do it quickly without thinking." What is wise?
o: Stop and think anyway
Do it quickly
Ignore the friend forever
Shout
questions.why: Rushing can cause hurt.

questions.q: Mina wants to go to the park but her little brother wants to stay in. What is a thoughtful way to choose?
o: Talk about each idea and find a plan that is fair
Do what the older child wants
Stay home and say nothing
Go alone to the park without telling anyone
questions.why: Talking finds fair plans.

questions.q: Put in order: choose well.
items: Look back at how it went
questions.why: We stop, think, pick, and learn.

questions.q: Is it wise to ask a trusted adult when you are not sure?
o: Yes
No, never
Only when happy
Only at night
questions.why: Trusted adults help us.

questions.q: What does a wise person do after a mistake?
o: Learn and try again
Pretend it never happened
Say it was someone else’s fault
Stop trying that thing for ever
questions.why: Learning from mistakes is wise.

panel.q: Two choices both seem good. What can help?
o: Ask which is kinder and fairer
Pick the first one you thought of
Pick the one that is easiest for you
Pick the one with a prize
panel.why: Kindness and fairness help us compare.

panel.q: Why can a rushed choice go wrong?
o: We may not notice who gets hurt
Because rushing always makes us too tired
Because quick choices are never fair
Because slow choices are always wrong
panel.why: We miss important things.

panel.q: Can a thoughtful choice still turn out badly?
o: Yes, we cannot know everything, but we can learn
No, a thoughtful choice is always perfect
Yes, but only because we were careless
No, if you think hard nothing goes wrong
panel.why: Thinking helps, but cannot give certainty.

teach.model: A thoughtful choice means stopping to think about who it helps or hurts. Then we pick and learn after. For example, returning a lost mitten.

stages.title: Asking why things happen
stages.hook: Why does the ice melt on a warm day? Why do we feel sad when someone leaves? Are all "why" questions the same?
explain: A why question asks for a reason. Some "whys" are about how things work, like why rain falls. Others are about people, like why a child is sad. Others are about right and wrong, like why we should be fair.
To find reasons, we can look, ask others, read, and think. Sometimes there is a clear answer. Sometimes people give different answers, and we keep thinking.
A good thinker says "because" and gives a reason. A good thinker also listens to other reasons. Asking why helps us understand the world and each other.

example.q: Why do we say thank you?
steps: Ask: what does thank you do?
It shows we notice kindness.
So the reason is: it shows care.
example.a: To show we are grateful and care.

analogies.home: A child asks why we wash hands. Because it keeps germs away.
analogies.nature: A child asks why leaves fall. Because the tree is getting ready for a new season.
analogies.city: A child asks why we stop at red lights. Because it keeps people safe.

stages.mnemonic: Why? Because! Say a reason, try, try.
terms: A cause or explanation for something.
A word that gives a reason.
Something that makes something else happen.
To feel curious and want to know.

misc.wrong: A "why" question always has one right answer.
misc.right: Some have one clear answer and some have many ideas to think about.

stages.limits: Some why questions are about nature and can be tested. Others are about values and people still discuss them.

trip.prompt: Find something that makes people curious.

questions.q: What does "because" give?
o: A reason
A colour
A game
A song
questions.why: It gives a reason.

questions.q: Which is a why question?
o: Why do birds sing?
Birds are small.
A bird sits.
Look at that bird.
questions.why: It asks for a reason.

questions.q: Why do we put on a coat when it is cold?
o: To keep warm
To be loud
To be tall
To be fast
questions.why: A coat holds in warmth.

questions.q: Why do we stop at a red light?
o: To be safe
Red is pretty
It is a game
Cars like it
questions.why: It stops accidents.

questions.q: Does every "why" have one answer?
o: No, some have many ideas
Yes, all why questions have one right answer
No, none of them have any answer
Yes, but only grown-ups know it
questions.why: Some are open for thought.

questions.q: Which "why" is about people being fair?
o: Why should we share?
Why is the sky high?
Why is water wet?
Why do stars shine?
questions.why: It is about how people should act.

questions.q: A friend gives a different reason from yours. What is wise?
o: Listen and think about it
Tell them their reason is wrong
Ignore it and keep your own
Say you will never listen to them
questions.why: Listening helps us learn.

questions.q: Match each why question to the kind of thing it asks about.
questions.why: Why questions come from many areas of life.

questions.q: Why do we keep asking "why"?
o: To understand more
To make other people stop talking
To show we know everything
To make the lesson last longer
questions.why: Asking helps us understand.

questions.q: You say "because" and give a reason. What does this show?
o: You are thinking
You are hiding
You are sleepy
You are lost
questions.why: Giving reasons shows thinking.

panel.q: A child asks "Why do people argue?" What is a good way to start?
o: Think of different reasons and ask people
Say it cannot be known and stop
Pick the first answer you hear
Ask only people who agree with you
panel.why: We can gather reasons and think.

panel.q: Why is it good to give a reason for your idea?
o: Others can understand and think about it
It helps others to understand us, and it also makes us win
It means we never have to listen
It proves we are right at once
panel.why: Reasons help others see your thinking.

panel.q: Can we keep wondering even when we find an answer?
o: Yes, new questions can come from answers
No, once we have an answer we stop
Only when a teacher says so
No, answers end all questions
panel.why: Good answers often lead to new questions.

teach.model: A why question asks for a reason. We say because and give a reason. Some whys are about nature and some are about people. For example, why do we say thank you?
